utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The witness is to be brought in. Good morning. Unfortunately our start was delayed by a technical problem, but apparently it is resolved now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. The affirmation you made to tell the truth still applies, and Mr. Popovic is continuing with his questions. Please sit down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: We will continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will ask the witness to be shown D180.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: It's your tab number 26, General. You can see the document, it's called proclamation to the citizens of Kosovo and Metohija. Are you familiar with it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: I know that a document with these contents was broadcast on the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the next page in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: I'll ask you to look at the last paragraph after the subheading "Albanians." It says: "Only living together without hatred and contempt leads to a happier future, a carefree childhood for our children, regardless of religion or nationality. Let us all together make an effort to restore peace to our lands. Return to your homes and your everyday work. Do so today." Was this something that was conveyed as a message to the Albanian minority in all of Serbia and in Kosovo and Metohija and does this date, the 7th of April, 1999, is it consistent with what you recollect?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have been very hesitant to intervene when there have been -- there has been quite a lot of leading questions in chief. But this one is leading and very badly leading, having regard to what the witness said in the previous testimony. In any case, in chief, counsel should ask the witness non-leading questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, I can't disagree for a moment with what you say, but Mr. Popovic is quoting a document. And was -- he then asked, Was this something conveyed to the Albanian minority. How is that leading?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, I think having regard -- well, he puts it to the witness as it were that it was conveyed to the Albanian minority. He leads him on that score. In his previous testimony he was saying that he was not sure that this document was even translated to Albanian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you speaking of testimony yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. In the 92 ter statement which is part of the record of his evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Carry on, please, Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Without wishing to go into a debate, I just read out a passage under the subheading "Albanians" and the text that follows. If this is not enough in terms of grounds for such a question, I will rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, would you look at this last paragraph and tell me to whom it was addressed?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: It's obvious that it was addressed to Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Did what I just read reflect the position of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia at that moment, and did it reflect their attitude to ethnic Albanians?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: Yes, this is a reflection of the attitude of the General Staff, but it was also quite obvious that only this road leads to proper solutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I now ask for D006-0287.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Your number 27. We see a document called "Briefing 27/99." The date is April 1999. Could you focus on bullet point 7 under paragraph 2, and it says: "According to foreign ex-pats, the operation of land forces could begin within 15 days, and it could involve around 100.000 soldiers." What was the reaction of the General Staff upon receiving information that a land operation could begin involving 100.000 troops?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: We followed closely all the developments concerning the possibility of lands operation. I told you that such information circulated in the media and in some intelligence sources. Of course, at that time we were not sure whether the operation would go ahead or not. We knew that within the NATO various options were being considered in the war against Yugoslavia including that possibility. However, we did not manage to learn whether the decision had actually been made to go ahead with the land operation. We were, therefore, forced to carry out preparations for any contingency, including that, because even as non-military experts can understand, the army takes some time to prepare, so we conducted partial mobilisation, training, and deployment of units on the axis where we expected a land operation could go forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the same page, the last paragraph reads: "In north eastern Albania, training camps, Bajram, Curri, Has, and Kuks were re-activated to train Albanian terrorists. Weapons for terrorists were being supplied to Albania and Macedonia." Can you comment briefly?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: Yes, this is one kind of information we received that such training was conducted in training centres in the north-east of Albania. Of course, we were sensitive to this issue, we monitored what was going on with these men who were being trained there, whether they were going to be sent into our territory, with what kind of objectives and assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see D006-89 and D006-0296. The first number in B/C/S and the second number in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: It's called land operations -- "NATO Land Operations Against SFRY." And here in item 2 it says: "In both options, the aggressor is reckoning on Siptar forces from the territory of Macedonia and Albania to spear-head the first echelon of ground forces. They are being armed, equipped, and trained at the moment." Can you tell us how topical this information was and were you expecting that to take place within a short time?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: Yes, this is what our information was and we were trying to predict what course it would take, if it happened. Our information that the first waves of attack across the FRY border would involve forces of Albanian terrorists from Albania and Macedonia. This was soon followed by an attack in Kosare by strong forces from Albania. However, they were rather unsuccessful with great losses on both sides and then they moved the focus of attack to the axis of Morina where they again failed to penetrate our territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D537, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P1331 will be our next document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Your tab 28. General, this is a session of the collegium of the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command held on 9 April 1999. We will look at page 2 in B/C/S and the same page in English. You say the proclaimed objectives of the aggression were, first, to prevent a humanitarian catastrophe, second to neutralise the military the power of the FRY, three to preserve the credibility of the US and NATO, while the real objective is punishing the FRY and forcing it to accept a peace agreement that would ensure the bringing in of NATO forces into Kosovo and Metohija and seizing that part of the territory from the FRY. Are these really the objectives as you presented them to the collegium, and did they prove to be indeed part of NATO strategy?

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have the wrong page in both languages. Page 2.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, let me say that this is one of the collegium meetings where we considered the situation in greater detail. I told you that during the war collegium meetings took place every day, but two weeks into the war, this was a proper occasion to consider the situation in greater detail. This presentation made is based on all my information that I gained thus far and the objectives, as I saw them, in their plans. We received that information from all sorts of sources, our operative intelligence sources, agents, and others. Most of these were -- had been implemented by that time or were being implemented. When I say that, I mean primarily the resolving of the status of Kosovo and Metohija and separating it from the territory of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at page 5 in both B/C/S and English.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: On page 5 you say: "The second option, if combat operations continue, is to bring in armed Siptars supported by NATO. This option is increasingly likely after the prospect of the planned withdrawal of the so-called Kosovo Liberation Army and the Siptar people from Kosovo and Metohija which has realistically created a difficult humanitarian situation." Could you explain this planned withdrawal?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: We had that information that in the movements of population there was an intent to portray them as a humanitarian catastrophe in the eyes of the international public, and when a large number of people find themselves in a relatively small area, it does look like a humanitarian situation. Indubitably, there were attempts to manipulate these people with I a view to achieving certain goals that they thought they could achieve that way and those objectives were continued bombardment and infliction of the greatest possible losses on the army and the police in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see page 8 in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: On page 8 in paragraph 3 in B/C/S and I believe it will be paragraph 4 in English you say: "Bearing in mind the earlier outlined aims and the cruelty of the aggressor, switching to the peace option would not be easy to achieve, but we are convinced that it is possible, and in that sense if we quickly make the right moves, there is room for real optimism."

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: We constantly sought to restore peace and to find a peaceful solution. Here I presented a variety of options how the situation could develop, and I unequivocally favoured the political solution, the peaceful solution. However, this did not happen. Instead, the war continued for another two months.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I now ask for D183.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Your tab 29. It's called "Directive to Engage the Army of Yugoslavia in Defence Against the NATO Aggression," dated 9 April 1999. On page 1, subheading 2.1, it says: "Aims and tasks of the aggression: To prevent a humanitarian catastrophe, to neutralise the military power of the FRY, and to maintain the credibility of NATO and the US, while the real objective is to inflict as heavy casualties on the VJ as possible, to force the FRY --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we slow down, please, both the counsel and the witness are going too fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, I will now ask you what the interpreters are asking us, namely to slow down. We are both speaking too fast. After my question, please wait a few seconds before you start answering, and I will try to slow down too. So your answer has not been recorded and you need to give us again your comment on 2.1.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: I think a comment is almost superfluous because it turned out, as the war went on, that what is written here came to pass.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 5 of this document, please. Page 6, paragraph 1, in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: In item 2 we see the concept and idea of strategic defence: "Engagement and use of the Army of Yugoslavia in defence against NATO forces should take place in two stages with complete implementation of the Geneva Conventions on international law of warfare and humanitarian law." Do you know that the Army of Yugoslavia developed certain documents to be given to every soldiers to educate them about the international law of warfare and international humanitarian law?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: Yes. Such documents were prepared. I must say, it was I who proposed at the collegium meeting that they be prepared. And they contained excerpts from international humanitarian law for officers and for servicemen. They were prepared in a useful format so that they could easily be carried on one's person in a pocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will move to the next document, please. D504. The number that might be easier is D008-2858.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can I inquire whether this one is notified, or noticed?

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I think you have been notified. There was an additional notification sent by the Defence on the 31st of January. Could we please see page 6 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: We see that it is a combat report; it's number 30 in your binder. It's combat report number 23, dated the 16th of April, 1999. On page 1 it said: "Under the guise of a humanitarian operation, the first part of main forces who should take part in the ground operation against Kosovo and Metohija are being brought into Albania." Was there still a real danger of a land operation in the area of Kosovo and Metohija on the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: Yes, at the time, there was still concern on our side that there might be a land operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please have a look at page 6. Under item 5, security situation in the Yugoslav army, in the second paragraph it reads: "The enemy attaches exceptional importance to psychological and propaganda activities. In order to justify the continuation of the aggression, in addition to stressing the humanitarian catastrophe and ethnic cleansing, he now also stresses documentation of mass graves which have allegedly been detected and located by satellites and mass rape." On the 16th of April, did you have any information that there were mass graves in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: No, at the time, as far as I remember, we did not have any information that would indicate that. I think that this is another example of how a problem, even if it existed, could be resolved differently through propaganda. That is to say that the information could be submitted to the state organs of our country, which would certainly take measures to that effect if it was determined that the information was correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see the next document, it's D006-0300.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: It is your tab 31.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But before we move to this document, Your Honour, I will tender the previous one because the number is not 3504, but the one I told you, D008-2858, if it could please be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Which document is that, Mr. Popovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's the document that we just discussed. It's the combat report number 23, dated the 16th of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D538, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now please go back to document D006-0300.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, this is the briefing 43/99, the date of this document is the 21st of April, 1999. Under item 5 it reads: "According to the available information, transport to Albania of 24 Apache helicopters and 18 VBR should be completed. As part of the reinforcements for the enemy forces in our region, around 300 members of the 82nd VPD of the US OS arrived in Albania. Parts of this division arrived in BH earlier, and the arrival of its members in Macedonia has been announced. According to our information, the Italian contingent, 2500 members, will also be completed today in Albania." So it was on the 21st of April. Could you please comment on this. Does this mean that there was mass bringing in of forces to the borders of FRY?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: Yes, following the reactions of the armed forces in our surrounding countries. We learned that the Apaches were moved from Germany to Albania which was later on confirmed in the media. The Apache helicopters are very efficient, and we were certainly afraid that they might be used because we would certainly have increased losses due to the attacks of these helicopters. Other elements of armed forces which are listed here also caused concern on our part if they were to be directly used in the area of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D539, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see document D006-0306. It's a Defence document.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, it is your tab 32. It is a report 47/99, the date of this document is the 25th of April, 1999. If you could please focus on item 8. "Manipulation with the Siptar refugees are continuing. They are being sent around in circles on the border between Macedonia and Albania which is organised by the CIA." Just a brief comment?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: It was another piece of information we received that the number of refugees was being represented as greater than it actually was.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please move on to the next page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Under "proposal," it reads: "Since we are manipulating the Siptar refugees and using them to justify the continuation of the aggression to public opinion, it might be a good idea to call on them again to return to their homes and reject the 'care' that the NATO member countries are providing for them." Here I would ask you to say primarily what was the character of these calls and did you really wish for these people to return to their homes?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: Firstly, we understood quite well what problems could follow on the basis of this manipulation with a great number of refugees, and that really caused dissatisfaction of the public which is quite normal, so we wanted, through this proposal, to stop this treatment of those people and to call on them once again to return to their homes. I cannot say whether that really happened or not, whether another proclamation was issued or not because I do not remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D540, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see the document D006-0107.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: It is your tab 34, General. General, it was a briefing held on the 30th of April, 1999, and under your name on the first page it says: "Activities were stepped-up for three reasons, the weather has improved, fuel tanks have been provided, on the eve of Chernomyrdin's visit." Could you please firstly explain to us the stepped-up activities; what does that mean? And then if you can please explain the third reason: "On the eve of Chernomyrdin's visit;" what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: The stepped-up activities meant firstly that the NATO air force was used and so were the cruising missiles. It is well known that the numbers differed during the war from 3 to 500 until 1.000 sorties, we noticed that at the time when the nights were clear in Belgrade, which was rare, that the activities were stepped-up. That meant that the number of sorties increased, as was the number of cruise missiles which were launched. We believe that this was additional pressure against our side and also against the mediators so that the conditions which had been imposed would be accepted as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D541, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see D006-0265. It is a Defence document, and it's your tab 35.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, this is report number 73, dated the 4th of May, 1999, under item 3. It says: "The military and political situation in Macedonia" --

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is on page 2 in the English version of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: You say the following: "We have obtained intelligence information that NATO has made a decision for a large number of Siptar refugees to be transferred to Macedonia, apparently because there are serious problems with the distribution of humanitarian aid due to abuse by local Albanian authorities. This implies new changes to the ethnic composition of Macedonia in favour of the Siptar minority. "During his recent visit to Macedonia, a senior military leader of the so called KLA, said that NATO leaders had told him that Macedonia is an artificial creation which should be divided and that the Macedonian authorities no longer existed, because the Alliance has a major say in making key decisions. On that occasion, he instructed Siptar nationals to direct all their activities, including refugees and operations of the so-called KLA, towards Macedonia." First of all, as you were the chief of the intelligence administration in the General Staff, do you know about the greater Albania project?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: The greater Albania project is well known to every citizen, I believe, because it has been public for a long time. Several versions are posted on the internet, and it was certainly familiar to us in the intelligence administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: And did this project of greater Albania include the territory of Macedonia and the ethnic Albanians who live there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: Yes, on the maps which are available --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It's leading. I mean, I hesitate to rise, but a lot of these questions are leading. I rise in respect to only some that might be controversial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They are controversial, are they, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Most of them are not, but occasionally, including this one, is controversial to a degree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you are aware of that subject matter, Mr. Popovic, if you could be careful not to lead in respect of it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will take that into account, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, I will then ask you to comment on the quotations from this paragraph which we just read out, and if you could tell us whether these predictions were confirmed in future?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: As for the greater Albania project, I already said a few words. I think this is something well known and generally known. In the western part of Macedonia, there was really a series of armed incidents between Albanian groups and Macedonian authorities. After that, peace was established on the basis of the Ohrid Agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D542, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, could we please see D006-0315.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: That is your tab -- just a second. 37. You can see that this is briefing number 64/99. The date of this document is the 12th of May. And if you could please focus on item 4, and if we can comment on it. I wouldn't read it out as it's a lengthy paragraph. If you can please read paragraph 4 and provide a brief comment, please.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: Yes. We presented the data that we obtained about the strength of NATO forces in the surrounding countries. This was confirmed later on. As I said yesterday, General Jackson at the Kumanovo negotiations confirmed that they had been in the area for three months already and that they were waiting to enter the territory of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please see the next page both in B/C/S and in English. If we could see the subtitle "Proposals" which read: "It is necessary to take several steps with good media coverage after talks with one of the international representatives who have good representation in the international community, and these steps need to be taken in a series that would show our willingness for a political resolution of the proposal." And under 2: "That the commission for the estimate of damage from the aggression should send a request to the UN and other relevant international institutions which would -- may enable them to see the degree of destruction and of the damage done to the civilians." If you could please make a brief comment.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: This was part of our continued resolution to try to find a peaceful solution and for refugees to return, so we even said that it was possible for our troops to withdraw. We wanted to show some goodwill for resolving the problem. As for the other proposal, it was the result of really widespread damage caused during this war and the wish that the international factors be involved so that the facts would be established, especially the suffering of the civilian population which was becoming more and more frequent.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will become Exhibit D543, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we please see D006-0262.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, it is your tab 36. This is report number 90 on the activities of Albanian OS and Siptar terrorist forces in the border area with Kosovo and Metohija. We'll only focus on the first sentence which reads: "In the north-eastern Albania in Papaj, Kocanaj, and Ragam, members of the so-called KLA, 1.500 of them in each of these places, are undergoing 15-day training under the command of NATO officers. The groups have been formed from Siptars, from the diaspora, and refugees from Kosovo-Metohija." According to your information, was there a link between NATO and the members of the so-called KLA?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: During the combat operations, we established a number of facts which testified to this link, and then, later on, in various documents and materials, it was undoubtedly confirmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I tender this document into evidence as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D544, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we please see D006-0243.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, it is your tab 38. This is report number 23 dated the 19th of May, 1999, which reads: "Through an indirect source, who is said to be reliable, we have acquired photocopies of the topographical maps, which the KLA gave to American representatives in Macedonia on the 15th of May, 1999. Drawn on the maps are the precise positions and co-ordinates of the Yugoslav Army and MUP units and also the areas which they are not allowed to target - areas where KLA units and Siptar refugees are situated." Could you please comment on this report. Are you familiar with it, and do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: Yes, we received this information from our sources on the ground, and it confirms what I just said about the co-operation and contacts between the NATO forces and the Albanians on the ground which was beyond a doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, the following five pages are the excerpts from these maps. I wouldn't dwell on each of these because of the time constraints, but were these maps enclosed with this report, the maps which can be seen as part of this document?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: Yes, of course, the maps were enclosed with the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender this document into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D545, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we please see the document Y016-2926. To make it easier for my colleagues from the Prosecution, it's number 4030 from their 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, this is the briefing on the 22nd of May, 1999. Under item 2 there are quotations of what you said. And what I'm interested in is where you say that there are four points of this disagreement --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter notes that this cannot be found in the document. Could the counsel please repeat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is well known that at the time a series of peace initiatives had begun in the international community and various mediators were trying to find some resolution and to end the war. There were various assumptions and various problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, I'm sorry to interrupt you, but because of the transcript, the question that I asked you was not recorded, so I shall repeat it. It is on page 1 under item 2, when the Major-General Krga -- that's dash number 5, and it says there are four key contentious issues, 1, cessation of bombing; 2, composition of forces; 3, withdrawal of VJ; and 4, raising of indictments. Could you now please continue with your answer.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: By that time, many initiatives had been raised in the national community to stop the war. All sorts of mediators raised different contentious issues. You see that one of them is cessation of bombing, that really meant the conditions that had to be met for the bombing to cease. Many advocated the idea that bombing should cease and then political negotiations would follow. On the other hand, NATO insisted that bombing would continue until all the said conditions have been met. Another point here is the indictments to be issued against political and military leaders of Yugoslavia that was already on the agenda, and the issue was debated whether indictments should be issued or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, this is the 22nd May, 1999, how did you view this issue of possible indictments, you and the intelligence administration of the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: Well, I must say we did not deal with the possibility of indictments too much. It's a legal issue. We focused on monitoring the military forces in the region. But it was clear to us that issuing indictments while the war was still going on would not contribute to terminating the war and restoring peace. It could only cause additional friction, mistrust, and discontent. We thought it would be better to establish an interface with Yugoslav authorities to find a peaceful solution, and there would always be enough time to raise indictments if needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: You said that issuing indictments was not an issue that you dealt with, but did you deal with -- did you read the indictments to see what's in them?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: Well, yes, when the first indictments appeared, it was a new development and of course we had to review them to see what's in them, but still the focus of our work were defence issues and monitoring the engagement of NATO forces and such.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask for this document to be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D546, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have D006-0320.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Your tab 39. This is briefing number 77/99, dated 25 May 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look at para 6. That's page 2 in B/C/S and in English. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: "Siptar refugees are becoming increasingly dissatisfied with the treatment they are getting in Macedonia. A rising number of refugees are returning. Yesterday, about 4.000 refugees re-entered Kosovo from Macedonia through the Djeneral Jankovic border crossing." Can I have your comment.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: This shows, again, the treatment these refugees were getting. They were coming back to the area held by our forces which means that they did not have any real fear from us. They did not fear that they could be targeted by us. We accepted that as a hard fact, and to the best of our ability, we tried to help them return to their homes or wherever they wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then under the subheading conclusion, para 1, it says: "We should not expect that the aggressor would lower the intensity of strikes, regardless of the Russian criticism of the aggressor's latest action. As long as a political decision enabling NATO to safely withdraw from the conflict is pending, the attacks will continue." Again, can I have a brief comment from you.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: Of course, already at that time even in NATO member countries there were many initiatives to stop the war. They were searching for a way to put the best face on it and to save the credibility of NATO, a concern that was present from the very beginning. Of course, there was internal disagreement. Some member countries advocated the soon-as-possible cessation of attacks, whereas other countries thought that intensive strikes should continue until the authorities in Belgrade accept all that was demanded of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will become Exhibit D547, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D006-0325 will be our next document.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Your number 40. Briefing number 78/99. 26 May 1999. Paragraph 2, passage number 3: "Up to 1200 hours, a total of about 420 sorties were registered, including about 325 flown by combat aircraft, including long-range B-52s and B-1B bombers, which is more than average, probably due to favourable weather conditions but also to put pressure at a time of intensive diplomatic initiatives. Announcements that the list of targets will be expanded to include food processing plants and silos were also made, with the aim of putting additional pressure and causing anger among the entire population." Now, can I ask you to clarify what kind of pressures were placed on Yugoslavia at the time of intensive diplomatic initiatives, and explain this reference to a broadened list of targets. What was that to include?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: We already noted through analysis that at the time of diplomatic initiatives, the number of sorties always increased. We saw that as a sort of pressure and a demonstration of the Alliance's readiness to go full hilt until their conditions are met. Some of the NATO moves were indicative of that, such as continuing to bomb a target that had already been destroyed. Also, some of them threw bombs into the Adriatic Sea after a completed assignment. We thought that that was a sign of their own displeasure that the war was continuing against the very unequal enemy. As for the broadening list of targets, we monitored this possibility to include civilian targets and references to possible inclusion of food processing plants and silos which would, of course, cause an environmental catastrophe. It's a well-known fact that power plants were bombed and there was even mention of possible bombing of the nuclear reactor in the Vinca institute, and we thought that even the possibility of bombing such targets was known to NATO planners to be a sure-fire way of causing outrage among the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I ask for this document to be admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D548, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now may I ask for D006-0258.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: It's your number 41, General. Report number 33 on KLA activities to procure arms. 29 May 1999. "According to information from a reliable source, a Siptar group was in France a couple of days ago to purchase weapons for the KLA. The group was most probably led by the newly-appointed chief of the KLA staff for Kosovo, Agim Ceku." This report is about the purchase of weapons for the KLA from various sources. Tell me, at that time, on the 29th of May, was this an on-going issue, the purchase of weapons for the KLA?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: This went on all the time. They were constantly looking for modern weapons. And after the war, all sorts of well-known foreign TV stations made programmes about this. We monitored those activities, but we never managed to detect all their channels and sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D549, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D006-0256 will be our next document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Tab number 42 for you, General. Report number 34 dated 31st May, 1999. In paragraph 2 we read: "According to this source, this well armed and organised group is repressing the Siptar population in order to recruit new fighters for the KLA and to drive the others from their homes and force them to become refugees." Your comment, please.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: Yes, this is another report that confirms the pervasive efforts to drive people from their homes and make them move out to create this picture of a humanitarian catastrophe.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can the document be received, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D550.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. D006-0329, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Tab 43 for you, General. Briefing number 87/99. June 1999. 4 June 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 2 in B/C/S and English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: The subheading reads: "Reaction to our acceptance of the principles." And it begins with: "The Italian Main Staff commented ..." Could you read it to yourself, General, and comment.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: Yes, in these reactions and comments by the Italian Main Staff, we see confirmation of certain things we mentioned before. First of all, it is confirmed that many NATO member countries were inclined to stop this war as soon as possible. Second, it also turned out that there had indeed been a lot of disagreement among the allies concerning the conditions on which the war should be stopped. And it is very indicative and noteworthy to see this announcement that the situation will change considerably in favour of the Albanians once the Yugoslav security forces withdraw, that is, the MUP, and the KLA will be strengthened. I must say, we did expect that with the army and MUP withdrawal from Kosovo, the KLA would be disarmed and only the KFOR would remain in place. However, we all know now that this didn't happen. A protection force was established from these forces, and now the security forces of Kosovo are taking over. This has unfavourable repercussions on the peace in the region. General Jackson who visited Belgrade twice and talked to me in detail told me that they had opted for this decision in order to keep under control these armed Albanian groups in the framework of the Kosovo Protection Corps. If they had disarmed them, they would not have complied anyway, and they would have only continued to be a problem. But we see that this situation continues to be complex to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask to -- may I ask this document be received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, as Exhibit D551.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now, may I ask for D006-0001.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Tab 44, General. Here we see, General, that pursuant to a decision of the Assembly of Serbia and after the peace plan of the European Union and the Russian Federation has been accepted, a team of the Army of Yugoslavia is authorised. We see the members of the team, and your name under number 6. Then it goes on to say that: "On behalf of the Army of Yugoslavia, the team is authorised to hold negotiations with the authorised representatives of NATO and the armed forces of the Russian Federation on all issues pertaining to the implementation of the European Union and Russian Federation peace plan and to sign documents relating to the withdrawal plan of units from the territory of Kosovo and Metohija." First of all, let me ask you, were you indeed on this team that conducted negotiations on this peace plan? And then explain the nature of the peace plan that was eventually signed.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: Yes. As we can see here, I participated in these negotiations from the 6th to the 9th of June, 1999. The nature of the document signed was indicated in its name, military technical agreement. The members of the army that took part in the negotiations with the KFOR were not authorised to conduct political negotiations. Political negotiations had been completed earlier at the level of Mr. Ahtisaari, in the state leadership of Serbia; and the decision to accept this initiative was ratified by the Assembly of Serbia and the Government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. And we soldiers only had to carry out the technical aspect of the agreement. I must say that our counter-parts in the KFOR headed by General Jackson treated us professionally as colleagues with whom an important job was to be done. They treated us fairly. They did not push us to the wall to accept any concessions that we had not been prepared to accept. The first version was not accepted because we insisted some provisions needed to be changed, such as the breadth of the land zone, and that's why negotiations took three days. The greatest stumbling point was the resolution of the UN Security Council. We insisted on the recognition of that resolution, whereas the KFOR representatives, including General Jackson, tried to persuade us that we were representatives of a sovereign state and we were entitled to agree to the entry of international forces in our territory. The very fact that we were able to insist on certain points is proof enough that these negotiations, while the war was still going on by the way, were rather fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know how many troops of the NATO Alliance were on the borders of the FRY at the moment the agreement was signed?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: We were able to see these troops because we were on the base where some of them were deployed. 50.000 were ready to enter Kosovo and Metohija, although at that moment there were not exactly 50.000, there were just over 40.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, did you at any time in 1998 or 1999 learn of or see any plan at the level of the leadership of Yugoslavia, the military leadership of Yugoslavia to expel the Albanian population of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: With full professional, personal, and moral responsibility, I can say that I have never seen such a document, nor have I ever attended a meeting or a conversation where any of the influential people or officials would have mentioned anything of the sort. It is well known that dozens of thousands of Albanians were living at the time in Belgrade, the capital, that they still live in the southern areas of Serbia, and neither during the conflict nor at any time before or later was there any intention to drive them out. The only plan was to resolve whatever problems we had in a civilised manner, politically. This was a constant in our policy. And this is still the prevailing sentiment in the General Staff in the army as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is the end of my direct examination. I have no further questions of the witness, and I see it's time for the break. And, yes, one more thing before I finish, I would like to tender this last document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document will become Exhibit D552.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will adjourn now and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: One of the documents you were shown earlier today is D180.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could it be brought up.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is a proclamation of the citizens of Kosovo-Metohija. I think you said you suggested that it be circulated. I just bring it up to remind you what we are talking about. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good. Now, do you remember that you were cross-examined about that by Mr. Hannis when you came here to testify in 2007?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I would just like to refer briefly to what you said about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we now could move to D520. That's the transcript of the witness's testimony that was received in evidence under Rule 92 ter. I should point out now that I'm on my feet and it crossed my mind, Your Honour, that Defence had tendered two documents, one under seal and an unredacted version. And I think D520 is the unredacted version. In any case, could we move to page 16904 of that transcript. That is the number on the transcript itself. I'm not sure of the e-court number.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Close to the bottom of the page at line 10, Mr. Hannis asked you to look at 3D753. That was the exhibit number in that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, for the record that exhibit is the same as D180 in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And he asked you at line 18: "Do you know when this was created and who created this particular document?" You said: "As far as I know, it was created around that date, and that is the date of the document. It was broadcast in the media, that can be checked. But as I said, I can't vouch for the authenticity of the text myself because I didn't work on it myself, so I can't say how authentic it is." And he went on to ask you: "Well, can you you show us or can you point out to us where there's evidence, hard evidence, that it was actually circulated to any of the persons that might have an interest in it or be affected by it? First of all, where is the version in the Albanian language? Is there one?" And you said --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is on the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So he asked: "First of all, where is the version in the Albanian language? Is there one?" And you said: "I really wouldn't know that. Of course there should have been, but whether there was or there wasn't, I really don't know." So that evidence remains -- or it is your evidence today or yesterday that that evidence is true?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: Yes, yes, of course it's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you personally know how, if at all, this was circulated?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: I know that it was circulated in the media, but whether it was distributed in any other way as leaflets or posters on walls, I really wouldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You would agree with me, General, that once war begins, and indeed in the build-up during the war, there's a certain degree of propaganda that is created and published by both sides?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: In principle one might give a positive answer, but I must say with full responsibility that we had absolutely no time to deal with any sort of propaganda, but, rather, all the steps that we proposed and made were made, frankly, with the intention to resolve the issues that existed and to resolve everything that our initiatives were focused on. So as for this document, there was no propaganda intention, no trick or deception behind this, but really a wish to neutralise what was very present in the international media about a humanitarian catastrophe. And for us this would have been the best option had the Albanians accepted to return to their homes. By that, this great problem of humanitarian difficulties that they were faced with would have been neutralised to a great degree. I agree, and I can confirm that it would be good if this had been published or broadcast in Albanian and in English and in Macedonian so that this would cover all the aspects of the crisis.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I suspect you are telling me that your side did not engage in war propaganda; is that your position?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: As far as I know, our side did not intentionally engage in war propaganda --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: -- aimed as causing any sort of confusion or anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we look at D543 briefly, please. And if we could go to the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: D543 is one of these briefings on the 12th of May that you or your staff put together for you, according to your evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could just look at the last page very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This proposal 1: "Several moves must be made one after the other with good media coverage (after talking to some of the international representatives with good standing in international community) to show our readiness for political solution to the conflict, the return of refugees, withdrawal of units, et cetera." Let me put it this way, you would agree with me that your side, during the conflict, sought to make use of good media coverage to achieve its purposes? Yes, do you agree or not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: I agree that the interest of our side was to be adequately represented in the media, but that did not necessarily have to imply propaganda.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: While we are on this document, I think you told us that these briefings were drafted for you in preparation for your presentations at the collegium meetings and at other meetings of the Supreme Command or the General Staff. Is my understanding correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: Yes, the briefings were prepared for my presentations at the meetings which were held daily. These were the meetings of the Supreme Command staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I'd like to just go back to something you said when you were last here, when you were being asked questions by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if we could return to that exhibit, the transcript. I think it's D520. Page 16855.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Starting at line 17. Or let's start from line 11 to get the entire question. You were asked: "You testified yesterday about the various sources of information you had in the intelligence administration. You've said that that included communiques from the state officials from the major countries. You also used partially media reports. You used sources from military and civilian diplomacy and various operational sources. What do you mean by 'operational sources'?" You said: "Well, you probably know that every intelligence service, in addition to public sources and the technology, has operative sources, that is, agents of different categories and different levels." Then you were asked: "And were any of these paid agents, paid by the army intelligence?" Your answer was: "There were all sorts of agents, but the paid ones were easily in the minority because we didn't have much money to pay them." And you were asked --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if we could move on to page 18656.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: "Based on your years of intelligence work, would you agree me that some of those sources from whom you got intelligence had to be viewed with a certain amount of skepticism or you would take their information, as I would say in my language, with a grain of salt; correct?" And your answer was: "Absolutely, I think that applies to all intelligence services in the world." And that remains your testimony; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Notwithstanding that, that some information may be incorrect, I'd ask you about a couple of these briefings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we look at D524. D524, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is a General Staff report on intelligence -- on KLA intentions of the 9th of March --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. D524 is the document with Defence number D008-3977. We have it here now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let me read from your testimony yesterday in respect of this document, and this is at page 10568, line 8: "Unfortunately, everything that was indicated here actually happened, kidnappings, killings, media propaganda, recruitment of new members, et cetera." The document states that the KLA with foreign assistance had drafted plans for staging a massacre of innocent Albanians and members of the OSCE which would provide a legal basis for activating the forces to extract the verifiers, and thus entry of a NATO KOV into Kosovo and Metohija. That part of it I had a little bit of concern. Was there a massacre of members of the OSCE; did that actually happen?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: There was no major incident such as the one in Racak, but there were individual attacks and murders in various places, but not a major incident such as the one in Racak, as far as I remember. This did not happen at this period.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Maybe I'm not asking the question with proper focus. You said yesterday that everything that was stated in this report actually happened, and I'm looking in the report and seeing -- one moment.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: As far as I remember, the Defence counsel asked me about the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Let me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm not sure if there is a need for me to react, but the witness's answer was not that everything that is included in this report happened. In his answer, the witness stated what did happen and mentioned certain things such as kidnappings and murders and so on, so I believe that the question that he confirmed that everything that is mentioned here happened is not really correct because he did not say that during the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Krga, during your examination-in-chief referring to this document you said everything -- unfortunately everything that was indicated here actually happened, kidnappings, killings, media propaganda, recruitment of new members, et cetera. Do you see paragraph 1 of this document referring to kidnapping and killings?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you see in paragraph 2 it says here that "the KLA, with foreign assistance, are drafting plans for staging a massacre of innocent Albanians," --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: We had --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, no, you see, the question now is -- or let me read -- I wish to ask you about the kidnapping of members of the OSCE. May I just say that I see from a clear reading of paragraph 1 of the report that counsel's intervention was correct, I can see that. You said here the KLA with foreign assistance has drafted plans for staging a massacre of innocent Albanians and members of the OSCE verification mission. Did you receive information that the KLA had a plan for massacre of members of the OSCE?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: In the reports which we sent to other users, each passage was written on the basis of some kind of information or report which we received from various sources, including the ones that you just mentioned. There is not a single sentence here that is not --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you communicate that to any member of the OSCE that there was a KLA plan to massacre them?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: As far as I remember, we did not; but we did inform the organs on the ground, the 3rd Army and Pristina Corps Commands which were in contact with them, but I cannot claim whether they informed them about this or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you ascertain what is the nature of this foreign assistance for the massacre of OSCE verifiers?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: We did not continue any investigation to establish whether this was true or not. It says here that these were the plans, so this does not necessarily mean that every plan will be carried out. We received information that there were such plans, and this is why we notified those who are listed here to take certain measures so as to ensure that this plan would not be carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. General Krga, please -- thank you for the information, but can I just ask the question again. Did you ascertain what is the nature of this foreign assistance for the massacre of the OSCE verifiers? Who are these foreign elements or factors involved in this plan?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: From this point in time, I cannot remember with any reliability whether anyone was mentioned by name or by institution that would make it more precise. We just mention it here in general terms, we just said foreign elements, and I really can't remember any more than that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you remember where you got this information from? What was the source of this information?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: We daily received 100 or more reports and I really cannot remember who the source of this one was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let's look at D550. And it's the same question I want to ask you about the source of these reports that entered into your briefings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: D550 has Defence number D006-0256.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And this is information that you obtained through what you describe here as intelligence work about the activities of the KLA in Kotlina. Do you know the source of this information -- the original source of this information?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: After 11 years, I really find it difficult to remember who was the operative source by first and last name or what was the structure that forwarded this information to us. I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, can I just ask you a couple of questions about the system. Basically this information might have been received within the system by a variety of different sources on the ground, maybe an agent who whisper it, maybe electronic reception devices, it could be a variety of means to obtain information of this nature; correct? You can't nod, you have to answer verbally. Is that correct what I just said?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is waiting for the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm waiting for you to finish, and then I will answer. Yes, you are completely right about what you just said that the source is -- the possible sources are very different. There are various.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you had various types of these sources within Kosovo and Metohija itself?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: Yes. In Kosovo and Metohija we also had varied sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So would field sources, for example, agents in the field report up to a field officer who will report up to a regional directorate that eventually would report up to you in the headquarters in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: Basically it was just as you now expressed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you recall generally about how many field agents you had in Kosovo itself?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: In Kosovo we had an intelligence outpost where there were several agents continually, but we also sent agents from Nis and from Belgrade and they would establish contact with their operative connections, so that the number varied quite a lot from one day to another.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: About how many agents would you have there continually in 1999 during the intervention?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: If I remember well, around five.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And these agents would have various sources of information on the ground in Kosovo? Each one of these agents would have various sources of information on the ground in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: Yes, in Kosovo and abroad, in foreign and neighbouring countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But the five agents that were continually posted in Kosovo in 1999, were they responsible for gathering information in places outside of Kosovo, or was their primary focus Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: It was their responsibility to engage operative sources in Kosovo and in south Serbia, to gather intelligence within Serbia and beyond its borders.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did they submit their reports up to you, or did they submit reports at all in writing?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Each of these reports was drawn up based on a written report. I mean, this report that we wrote at the head office. It was produced based on the reports of our agents.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You also had - I think it's your evidence, tell me if I'm correct - agents who were based in countries, in foreign countries?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: Naturally like other intelligence services, we had our sources in foreign countries as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let's look at a document you were shown, P1333. This is the minutes of the collegium of the General Staff of Yugoslavia on the 2nd of February. Page 14 in English, 13 in B/C/S. And you could focus on the bottom where Major-General Krga speaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said in a discussion about Russia: "I would like to add something" --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Counsel is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Popovic. The pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The page in B/C/S I don't think is the right one. The witness needs to follow. In the B/C/S version, we don't see the passage when Mr. Krga speaks. I believe it's page 12, only if we scroll up. I think this is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said: "As early as 1991, while I was an envoy there," and that's in Russia, "I said in reports to this effect that we shouldn't fool ourselves that Russia would support us in the manner in which ... Carried away by emotions, the Slavic soul, and so on. Russia is not ruled by the Slavs or the by the Orthodox people, it is ruled by Jews, who are in collusion with the Americans, and we cannot expect any support from them." Was this opinion which you expressed based on your own experience as an envoy or was it based on a report from intelligence sources?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: Well, that's my experience from the time when I served there as a diplomat for three years. Many of our people who visited Moscow in those times of crisis were trying to establish a relationship with the Russians on these grounds that I mentioned here, Orthodox Christianity, common Slavic roots, et cetera. I was trying to say that all that doesn't matter, that one should not think in terms of those categories because Russia had changed and their leaders are guided by their own interests rather than imaginary categories like Slavic roots, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yeah, here you said they were ruled by Jews. That aspect, is that the result of your experience, or was it intelligence?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: Well, members of the Jewish community there had great influence on the authorities; they had a lot of power. That's the experience I had from my tenure in Moscow. When I said that, I meant primarily the then-minister of foreign affairs of Russia, Mr. Kozyrev who often times stated publicly and showed in many ways that he was talking to others in regard to the Yugoslav crisis rather than worrying about our interests.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So you would agree with me that this comment of yours, at least to some degree, reflects your attitude towards ethnic issues?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: No, by no means. My view when ethical -- ethnic issues are concerned is quite clear. I do not discriminate on the grounds of ethnicity. This was just a caution, a warning to those who were expecting that Russians were going to help us as a brotherly Slavic nation as Orthodox Christians. I was just trying to say that when the Russians are concerned, we have to be more realistic in our expectations of support.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, let's move on. You referred to information you received of Kosovo Albanians returning home, I think, one of the documents you were shown. There was an indication that there were some 4.000 Kosovo Albanians who had re-crossed into Serbia. It's a document dated the 25th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you remember this source, the original source of that information?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: I really can't recall the original source of that information. 11 years later, you will understand, it's not easy to recollect every detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you, while you were in Belgrade during the NATO intervention, become aware of how many Kosovar Albanians had crossed the border into Albania and Macedonia in March, April, and May?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: I don't understand. Is that a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, I'll ask it again. While you were in Belgrade in 1999 during the NATO intervention, did you know how many Kosovo Albanians had left Kosovo to Albania and Macedonia in March, April, and May?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: As you know, there was all sorts of information and all sorts of figures circulating. I was not able to know to what extent the media exaggerated the numbers. I don't think that anybody had real numbers. We were simply that kind of situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you or anybody in the government at the time make an effort to get information from the United Nations High Commission for Refugees, from the office of the High Commission for Refugees?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: My service and I did not seek this data. I'm not sure about others. Of course, it sounds logical that somebody should have sought that information. But you will understand that the service I was heading had its hands full monitoring the attacks of the NATO Alliance against us. That absorbed all our time and all our attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know, just as a ball-park figure, that by the 25th of March when you referred to some 4.000 refugees returning home, that by that time approximately 800.000 Kosovo Albanians had left their homes? Sorry, withdrawn. The document you were shown, D547, when you spoke about 4.000 persons returning home, 4.000 Kosovo Albanian refugees returning home, that was not dated in March, it was the 25th of May, very close to the end of the conflicts, when there were some negotiations in place. Will you agree with me that by then, by then some 800.000 Kosovo Albanians had already crossed the border going in the opposite direction?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: I cannot quite agree because I am not aware of that precise figure, whether it's exact or it's a little less or a little more, I could not confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm giving an approximation. You knew that somewhere in that region, 7-, 800.000 Kosovo Albanians had left their homes, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: I knew that there were many of them, and to me 1.000 would still have been too many.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Counsel is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic -- Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Just regarding the record and the interpretation, lines 13 and 14 are not quite what the witness said. The witness exactly said "whether it's exact or it's a little less or a little more," not just "whether it's exact or it's a little more." We can also check the tape if necessary.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did mention the whole answer, "whether it's exact or a little less or a little more."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Carry on, please, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said yesterday in respect to the BBC News report of the 1st of April that you were shown - which is D532, so maybe you could bring it up - that these press conferences, instead of being taken seriously, were usually just one more piece of information which we had to verify and check it out ourselves. And very often we found that incorrect data and untruths were being presented. 10596. What sort of checks would you make when or if you heard news reports of massacres committed by Serbian or forces of the FRY in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: I recall reports that 100.000 people, for instance, were killed in Kosovo, and reports that there was an operation conducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We heard that yesterday that there were these reports which weren't true. And I'm not here saying that everybody report that was issued by anybody during this war is true. I'm just asking you what were these checks; you said you had to verify and check it out yourself. What was the nature of the verification process and the checking process when you received reports that there were massive crimes committed by forces of the FRY in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: I've already said that it was not our principal work to deal with events in Kosovo-Metohija. Our job was done primarily outside the borders of Kosovo. And in Kosovo-Metohija we focused on the KLA. I can't say that we took every report and every press conference someone held and then ran our own checks. We couldn't do that. We had too much to do with regard to the combat activities of foreign countries against our country. Maybe these reports were checked by someone else, I cannot say for sure. You know that we also had the security service of the Army of Yugoslavia that dealt with those internal security issue; we had the Ministry of the Interior; there were authorities on the ground. I suppose they were more involved in that kind of issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, for the time being I'm only asking you about what you said yesterday in respect to the BBC report on the screen before you. You said: "... press conferences like that being just one more piece of information in which we had to verify and check out ourselves." Can I take it from your answer now that you were not responsible for and you did not participate in checking out these things, these reports?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
