utterances.text: Formally speaking, it was not our job to check such reports. If we had been able, we, of course, would have checked them. We checked some information emanating from these press conferences through our intelligence sources in other countries to confirm or to discard, but we did not react to every press conference by launching an inquiry or an investigation. It would have been impossible with our capacities.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we look at this one, there is something very important and very concrete referred to in this one that I would imagine that you check it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If could you scroll down this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'll read it: "Major-General John Drewienkiewicz, former head of the OSCE's Kosovo Verification Mission, gave moving details of the refugee exodus from Kosovo. He said there was evidence that ethnic Albanians had been beaten, robbed, raped, and murdered all over the Serbian province. He added that there were reports of a mass grave near Prizren." Now, this is not a general thing, this is something concrete, a mass grave near Prizren. Did you check and verify that report? Whether it was correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: No, we did not engage our resources to check this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said earlier that you had the Ministry of the Interior, there were authorities on the ground, was it the responsibility of the Ministry of the Interior to check these allegations, especially something as concrete as an allegation of a mass grave in the vicinity of Prizren?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to speak on behalf of the Ministry of the Interior but I suppose if they had been interested -- but I suppose they were interested in this report and wanted to check it, not only they, but the units on the ground, I mean army units.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I mention the Ministry of Interior because you referred to them earlier indicating that they would be the ones interested in checking that. We have evidence before this Court from some of the people who participated in burying or disentering the bodies of Kosovo Albanian civilians from two mass graves in the vicinity of Prizren. Did you, during the war, know that these two mass graves existed?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: No, no, I really didn't know about the existence of those mass graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We have evidence before the Court that during a joint police/military operation in Meja in April 1999 upwards of 300 Kosovo Albanians were killed by Serbian security forces. Were you aware of that during the war in 1999?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: No, I say once again that my focus of activities was on following foreign armed forces, rather than the incidents on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We have evidence before this Court that on or about the 26th of March, 1999, in the vicinity of Suva Reka -- not in the vicinity of Suva Reka, in Suva Reka town itself, an entire family, but mostly the women and the small children of that family, dozens of them, were massacred by Serbian security forces. Some of their bodies were transported to Prizren, and later on some of them were found in mass graves in Serbia itself. Did you, during the war, know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: No, I really did not have any information about the crimes you mention.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What is striking is, one, we have evidence before the Court presented by the Defence that responsible people, Major-General Drewienkiewicz spoke about the mass grave near Prizren; we have evidence from victims that the persons, woman and children mostly I remind you, killed in Suva Reka were killed in broad daylight in the town itself; and we have evidence before the Court that this killing at Suva Reka was also broadcast in the international press. Whose responsibility would it be to verify and check the truth of these reports? Would it not be the MUP of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: I really cannot talk about who had what legal obligations among other institutions that were part of the state administration or the state in general because I don't know the details of all this. Each institution had its legal authority and also rules according to which it behaved during the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: According to your knowledge and experience as a general formerly in charge of intelligence and intellectual as well, I say that because of your education and training, was it not the MUP that was responsible to investigate these allegations, to verify and check these allegations?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: Well, based on general ideas about this, one could say that the Ministry of the Interior and the organs of power on the ground and whoever was there were all responsible for what you are talking about. But let me say once again, I cannot assert that and, above all, I do not have at my disposal any documents on the basis of which I could say anything of that sort with any reliability.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You testified earlier that you read the MOS indictment -- sorry, withdrawn. You testified earlier that you read the indictment that become public on the 27th of May against President Milosevic, President Milutinovic, and others; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: I was basically informed about the indictment through the media, but I did not have the document as such at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Didn't you say earlier that you read it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: No, as far as I remember, I didn't say that I read it, but that I was made aware of it by the media and in conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think you said that when the indictment appeared, you had to review them "we had to review them to see what's in them." You recall that, that you had to review them to see what's in them?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: No, I really did not review the indictment as a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. I'm referring to page 21, lines 22 to 25. But were you at least aware at that time that the indictment cited specific instances of crimes allegedly committed by forces of the FRY and Serbia?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that at the time either. I knew that the subject of the indictment were the crimes allegedly committed by the forces of FRY in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, but I did not know anything about the specific locations, the number of victims and so forth. I did not know the details about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What, if any -- or, I'll ask a general question so you could speak and describe fully what I want to know about. What were the lines of communications that your department, intelligence gathering, had with the MUP for Serbia? Did you exchange information with them, and if so, by what means?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: The information which was presented here shows that when we assessed that the MUP structures could be interested in specific pieces of information, then we would forward that to the MUP organs. Let me note that at the time within the Ministry of the Interior, there was also the state security service which was later separated and became the security and intelligence agency, so we mainly directed the reports to them. And occasionally, when there was information that had to do with the army and the units, we would receive that from them, but that was rare.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you go to Kosovo during the NATO intervention?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: No, I did not go there during the war. I only went once to Nis which is a town in southern Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you meet with Mr. Djordjevic during the war?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you know him up to the time of the war?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic was performing a high duty. He was a public personality, so to speak, and of course I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can I take it from your answer that as a senior member of the army you would, of necessity, have had to have some sort of professional association with him? You knew him in his capacity as chief of the public service department?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: Well, I said I did know him as someone who was a public figure, but we did not socialise then or later, simply each one of us had his own preoccupations, and professionally we did not have many contacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we look at D523. And I'm moving on to something else, Your Honours. If you could move to page 16 in the English, which is page -- I am sorry, I don't think I have the page in B/C/S. But if we could find in the Serbian version the last paragraph before paragraph 2.2.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Having read that, General, just the last paragraph before 2.2 begins, will you agree with me that by early 1999 - this is a document of February 1999 - the FRY leadership, the Serbian leadership was aware that ethnic tensions were running high in Kosovo and there was a real risk that Serbs in Kosovo as well as elements within the security forces may commit crimes against Kosovo Albanians?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: From the paragraph you mentioned, there is no crime that would follow. It follows that, as I noted, there was a likelihood that the Serbian and Montenegrin population might organise themselves to defend themselves, not to commit crimes. Now, of course, in armed conflicts, various things may happen. And this is why I formulated it that way in order to note that and to remind those responsible to take measures to ease the tensions so that this would not happen, so that murders, liquidations, kidnappings wouldn't continue because such things then cause reactions, that is, the effect of the spiral of violence in war when one act of violence causes another, and we saw what this led to. So this was really a sincere intention to do something as a preventative measures so that what I talk about here would not happen or would not keep happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But you were aware of the risk of self-organised Serbs as well as security force members attacking Kosovo Albanian people in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you have an answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Firstly, the security services do not do this self-organisation. They are state services which are precisely organised. And when we talk about citizens, I noted here the possibility that they might organise themselves in order to defend themselves to put up resistance, so as a reaction to crimes against them or any other activities that might jeopardise their lives and property. And my assessment was, as you can see in the last part of the sentence, that this might further complicate the existing situation in Kosovo-Metohija and make it more complex, and that was why I brought this up.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: General Krga, I suggest to you that the leadership of the FRY in Serbia took advantage of this prevailing situation, this obvious danger, to put in place a plan to expel the Kosovo Albanian population or a substantial portion of that population as a solution to the problems they were having there.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: Was that a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. I suggest that to you. Do you accept that or do you reject that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: I cannot accept your claim, because I said that I have not seen a single document that would indicate anything like that, nor was I ever present during a single conversation that would point to an intention to expel the Albanian population. I really believe that there is no authority with any responsibility that could ever presume to expel a million and a half Albanians or whatever their number was without the international community reacting to that. I believe that something like this really did not exist. And never in a single document, and I have seen thousands of documents, did I see anything of the kind that you are saying now. And I'm telling you that with full responsibility, with my moral and professional responsibility. So that is what I assert to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You wouldn't, would you, General, expect such an illegal plan to be documented, would you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: Well, in principle, there could be some virtual plans, but I'm telling you that I never saw a written document nor did I ever hear a conversation to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, I have nothing further in examination. Your Honour, may I just indicate that the Prosecution, of course, relies on the evidence which is part of the evidence in this proceedings, that is the evidence in the previous proceedings tendered under Rule 92 ter, in particular the cross-examination of this witness, as with any other. There are documents that were used in the cross-examination which, when one reviews the evidence, these documents are noted with the exhibit numbers of the prior case. All of them that the Prosecution wants the Court to take cognizance of have already been entered into evidence, so I will not be seeking to enter -- or tender any of them, but they have different exhibit numbers now in this case. I could read them to the Court, but I think, as a general principle, maybe a system could be found to facilitate the review of this material by the Court when it comes to review the totality of the evidence. Maybe I should just ask if it's necessary at this point to read out the present exhibits numbers of those document that were used in cross in the previous case?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: As to the general question, Mr. Stamp, clearly a cross-referencing of exhibit numbers would be of benefit both for final addresses and for the Chamber's deliberation, and a table of that cross-referencing would be, therefore, very helpful. I do not know if counsel have discussed this between them because you could also facilitate cross-examination and examination. I suggest there should be some discussion and the matter then raised again. The second part of your question is the particular exhibits today. If you plan to rely on particular exhibits today, it would help us and it could well help Mr. Popovic if you could read into the transcript now those documents upon which you rely with the two exhibit numbers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see counsel on his feet. I don't know if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I am sorry, Mr. Popovic, I thought you were standing there nodding agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I certainly agree with some points. But, first of all, I think that my colleagues from the Prosecution and we as a Defence should make an agreement about how to continue doing this. This sort of practice would cause some problems for the Defence, primarily because the exhibits which were used during the cross-examination of the witness in the Milutinovic case would not be presented here, which was the practice with all the documents that were used for the cross-examination of Prosecution witnesses when the Defence tendered each document that was used during the cross-examination at the time. For the simple reason that this Trial Chamber would have insight into these documents, and also that we could present these documents to the witness again so that he would give every answer to each of these documents. And in addition to this, there is another problem with this, and it is that the cross-examinations and then the redirects of witnesses which already testified in different cases were conducted by counsels for the Defence by six Defence teams, and if this system was accepted, then the Defence would also need to submit a number of other documents which represented the redirect or response to the documents which the Prosecution used during their cross-examination. And I think that thereby some confusion would be created in the case in connection with the exhibits and the weight they have and how the Trial Chamber would weigh them. So I think that during the break it would be best if we could consult with our colleagues from the Prosecution and then see what position we might take on this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I make it clear that the transcript has been received in evidence in this trial and is popularly relied on by both Defence and Prosecution for their respective purposes, and where relevant will be referred to by the Chamber in its deliberations and decision. In this case, we are told that all exhibits relevant to this case, all documents relevant to this case that were the subject of cross-examination and examination in the previous evidence are already exhibits before us. So there is no problem of exhibits not being before us that are relevant. That, at least, is what I understood from Mr. Stamp. Whether that was confined to cross-examination or whether it extended beyond that to re-examination, I do not know, and that certainly could be the subject of discussion between counsel. We would take the view, to make it clear, that, A, it would be helpful to have a cross-referencing between exhibit numbers in this trial and documents that are referred to in the transcript of witnesses. Secondly, that if there is a document dealt with in the previous trial that is considered to be material by either party, they should consider whether or not it is tendered in this trial. If it is not, we will not be taking it into account. Is that enough to help you in your discussions? We have reached a time now for the second break. We will adjourn and resume just after 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. As indicated by the Court or directed by the Court, it would only be the documents that are exhibited in this case that would be considered by the Chamber. What I propose to read now is just a cross-reference of the documents that are associated with this testimony in MOS that were used by the Prosecution in MOS which are already exhibits in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you mean Milutinovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry, forgive me. When I say "MOS," I mean the Milutinovic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It would be fancier if you used Milutinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. I'm so sorry. So this is a cross-reference of the Milosevic trial case numbers or exhibit numbers to the case numbers, exhibit numbers in this case for the documents used in cross-examination of this witness. The document Milutinovic et al. Exhibit 3D934 is D539. Milutinovic et al. document 3D898, is D528 in this case. Milutinovic Exhibit P941, is P1341 in this case. Milutinovic et al. Exhibit P935, is P965 in this case. Milutinovic et al. Exhibit P939, is P902 in this case. Milutinovic et al. P938, is P1339 in this case. Milutinovic et al. P1878, is P1328 in this case. Milutinovic et al. P1487 is P1236 in this case. Milutinovic et al. P1966, is D00104 in this case. Milutinovic et al. P1999 is P933 in this case. And Milutinovic et al. 3D692 is D219 in this case. I think that's it, Your Honours. But may I just have a moment to cross-check one thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Lastly, Your Honours, Milutinovic et al. document P1967 is D -- is D00105 in this case. Thank you, Your Honours. In due course, Your Honours, what is proposed is that the Prosecution will give a full cross-reference which we will provide to the Defence for their cross-check and subsequently file for the record. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That will be most helpful, thank you, Mr. Stamp. Now, Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this position of the Prosecution sets some tasks before the Defence because there were redirects in the Milutinovic case, and in these redirects, certain documents were are used that have different numbers in our case. Therefore, we will submit to the Trial Chamber the numbers, the documents used in the Milutinovic case that we should focus on when redirect transcripts are read from the Milutinovic case, and we will submit these in writing after we conduct redirect examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, in connection with your evidence today, I would like to show you D532 on the screen. [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We are not getting interpretation at the moment.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Technical error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's been corrected now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: If the question could begin again.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: I will repeat. How did you treat information that you received through press conferences such as the summary you received in this document?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: I've said already that we've had all sorts of experiences regarding information presented at press conferences. Often times, information presented at press conferences turned out to be inaccurate, and we lent less credence to sources of information like this as a result, less than we would have given them if they had proven to be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: So you are speaking based on your -- on the basis of your past experience with information presented at press conferences, that's your first sentence in the previous answer. Could you be more precise. Based on what experience and for what reason did you treat this information in that way?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: I believe I've already mentioned that there were all sorts of stories that at the beginning of the war 100.000 Albanians had been killed, that there were widespread rapes; and it was quite clear that this information and the numbers were exaggerated. And this led us to adopt the view of such information that we adopted.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, on page 54 of your testimony today, lines 1 through 5, the Prosecutor stated that the FRY and its leadership had a plan to expel ethnic Albanians in whole or in part to solve their problem there. And you give an exhaustive answer in the passage that follows. However, line 9 is a bit controversial in my view, maybe because of the way it was interpreted into English. Your answer in English begins with the words, in interrogative form, I don't know whether it's correct or not. The transcript reads "Can I not accept ..." That's why I want your answer to be given again, to avoid confusion.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, in response to that question, I said quite positively that I have never seen a document or attended any meeting where anyone mentioned expelling Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These were all my questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Mr. Krga, there are a few questions I wanted to ask you to clear certain things up in my mind, you understand. In answer to Prosecution counsel a while ago, you said that you were basically informed about the indictment through the media but you did not have the document as such at the time. You recollect this? Now, he asked you whether you had said earlier that you had read it and your reply was: "No, as far as I can remember, I did not say that I read it, but I was made aware of it by the media and in conversation." Do you recollect this?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: I want to direct your mind, Mr. Krga, to the evidence you gave yesterday when you said that: "When the first indictment appeared, it was a new development." And, of course, you had to review them to see what was in them. And my question to you now is what did you mean by review them to see what was in them?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: If I remember well, I believe that related to the first indications that there is an indictment and that there are indictments. I had reports that indictments were being prepared, and I believe that's what my answer pertains to, reports that there were indictments in preparation, but I really didn't see any indictments at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: You reviewed them to see what was in them, did you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: No, no. At that time, when the indictments were issued, I did not see them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: I see. Now, again, counsel for the Prosecution asked you earlier that while you were in Belgrade in 1999 during the NATO intervention, whether you knew how many Kosovo Albanians had left Kosovo for Albania and Macedonia in March, April, and May. And your reply was that as far as you knew there were all sorts of information and all sorts of figures circulating. You were not able to know to what extent the media exaggerated the numbers, and you didn't think that anybody had real numbers. You recollect this? Now, then, let me direct your mind to your evidence yesterday where you said in answer to Mr. Popovic that, as far as your proposal to set up admission points for refugees, you had previously recorded: "Their departure from the FRY and their return. They were moving in circles. And so we came to the conclusion that it would be good, a good idea ... to take back these people." Now, what did you mean that "we had previously recorded their departure from the FRY and their return"?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I didn't say that we recorded their departure or return, and we, I mean, we in our service really didn't do that; it wasn't our job. And the idea that they should be admitted back in an organised manner when they came back was first of all to relieve their suffering, and secondly to improve the image of Yugoslavia which was predominantly negative at the time in terms of treatment of refugees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me get it quite clear, you are saying that you did not say "we had previously recorded their departure from the FRY and their return" yesterday? You didn't say that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: I did not say that yesterday, and we did not do that. I don't know how it was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed. Thank you. Now, one last question, Mr. Krga, you said yesterday that depleted uranium was used in Kosovo in the NATO bombing and it was also used outside of Kosovo and the rest of Yugoslavia. You said that outside of Kosovo there were five locations where it was used, and, as Chief of the General Staff, you personally went there to evaluate the situation. Now, do you recollect this? Yes.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us what were those five locations outside Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: Those five locations were villages around the town of Vranje. One of them was Borovec I remember. I can't remember exactly those micro-locations, but they are in the immediate vicinity of the town of Vranje, between Vranje and Bujanovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Was there any mass exodus on account of those munitions there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: Those locations that we registered as locations where depleted uranium was used, we marked them and cordoned them off prior to decontamination so that citizens were aware of these locations. In most cases, those micro-locations are outside villages, outside populated areas, so that as far as I know there was no mass exodus on that account.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Mr. Krga, I thank you very much indeed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Just to follow-up on that last question, it's not clear to me when you are saying that the five locations, they were followed up, cordoned off, and marked, are you saying that happened as the weapons fell or at some time later? Can you help me there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: Generally speaking, during the war, we checked every location that was bombed by radiological detectors to see if there was any radiation; and if we found that depleted uranium munitions had been used we would mark it, we would mark such locations and cordon them off. And I cannot tell you now precisely whether it was on the same day or within three or five days, we tried to do it as promptly as possible, to the extent that we were able to in the conditions of air-strikes, continuing air-strikes. Now, detailed study and establishing the numbers, all that was done after the war. Cordons were put in place, the micro locations were isolated, and then we made plans for decontamination. It usually concerned territories where tanks or armoured combat vehicles were stationed because NATO tended to use this ammunition on these locations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What, then, led you as Chief of the General Staff to visit the five locations in Serbia but outside Kosovo? That would have been some three to four years later, if I understand your evidence correctly.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: Yes, we began decontamination later. We could not organise ourselves immediately because this is a quite complex technological process. So in agreement with the civil authorities, the Ministry for the Protection of Environment and the institute of nuclear technology in Vinca we set up teams which then carried out the decontamination. And at the time when I was the Chief of General Staff, this task was not yet completed. But it was almost completed and so I visited the members of the army who were charged with these tasks. I remember that I once went there together with the Minister for the Protection of Environment, that was Ms. Andjelka Mihajlov, I was on a visit together with her. So I was not directly charged with this; I was just visiting the area and supervising the work of our professional teams which were involved in this work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Mr. Krga, I do apologise, but I have a question, a bit tangential to the one my brother just asked you. Now, you said the refugees were returning to Kosovo which meant that they do not have any real fear that they would be targeted by the authorities. Now, did they have any fear of depleted uranium at all?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: I cannot say how much they knew about the use of depleted uranium, whether they were informed about this or not. It depends what part of Kosovo and Metohija they were returning to. What we managed to record, and we couldn't do all that precisely because we had to leave the territory of Kosovo, was that not all parts of the territory of Kosovo and Metohija were hit with this sort of ammunition, so that I really don't know to what extent the people who were returning were informed whether their village or town included any spot that was hit by this kind of ammunition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: So they wouldn't have left Kosovo because of depleted uranium, would they?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA Resumed
utterances.text: I couldn't say that. I could not answer with either yes or no. It is certain that they were aware at the time, both these people and the people living around the town of Vranje, what were the dangers of the ammunition with depleted uranium. Had they been fully aware that, they would probably have sought some short of shelter and wouldn't have remained close to that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You will be pleased to know that that completes the questions for you. The Chamber would thank you for your attendance here and for the assistance you've been able to give us. You are now, of course, free to go, and the Court Officer will assist you from the court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. Djurdjic will examine the next witness in the examination-in-chief, and I think he will have some proposals in connection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I think that my colleague Mr. Popovic should first propose the documents which the Defence has in its mind in connection with cross-examination in agreement with Mr. Stamp and inform the Chamber about the documents just like Mr. Stamp did. And I think that as we have gone this far in terms of time, my proposal would be to begin the examination-in-chief of the next witness tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, you are asked to fill in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will do my best, Your Honour. Now I will tell you what are the documents which the Defence used in the Milutinovic case during its redirect of this witness and which they noted during the examination. So we have a document which is 3D692 in the Milutinovic case, it is now the document D219. The document which has the number P1966 in the Milutinovic case is now Exhibit of Defence D104. Prosecution Exhibit from Milutinovic case P1967 in this case is registered as D105. Exhibit of the Prosecution P938 is in this case number P1339. And we still have one more exhibit, it's Exhibit 3D685 in the Milutinovic case, which is now registered as D523 in this case. I just don't know -- during the break the Prosecution and the Defence discussed this manner of tendering documents into evidence and we agreed that it should be so in this case, but I did not realise whether Mr. Stamp wishes this to be practice and that we should go on doing it that way or if it was only the case now, because as Defence we would have some difficulties with this as there is a great number of documents that have been used and also considering the facts that we don't have access to the documents in the same way that the Prosecution does in the sense of what is in e-court from the Milutinovic case. And, therefore, perhaps if lists were prepared in advance, that might facilitate things and allow both the Prosecution and the Defence to do this more easily. Now, whether at the beginning or at the end, I guess this should also be a matter of agreement, but I think we should reach some sort of consensus if this is a proposal on how to act in future. This is the only thing that was not quite clear to me at the end of our discussion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: From the Chamber's point of view, we accommodate what is convenient to counsel, but our present understanding is that there will be a composite list prepared cross-referencing the numbers of the exhibits in this trial which are also used in the Milutinovic trial in the course of material parts of the examination, cross-examination, or re-examination of a witness who is called here. So that if reading the transcript of the previous trial, counsel or the Chamber wishes to look at a document being referred to, the Chamber will have a cross-reference table to identify the number of the exhibit in this trial. Underlying that understanding are two propositions: First, if it is not an exhibit in this trial, the Chamber will not be referring to it, even though it may be referred to in the transcript in the Milutinovic trial. Second, it, therefore, follows that if either Prosecution or Defence want a particular document for the purposes of this trial, they will need to tender that document in the course of examination-in-chief or cross-examination so that it becomes an exhibit in this trial. And I'm sure, Mr. Popovic, that you can discuss with Mr. Stamp and overcome any inconvenience you may have in obtaining access to a document that was used in the Milutinovic trial and which may not presently be readily available to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The majority of the Chamber is persuaded to Mr. Djurdjic's eloquence and takes the view that we should adjourn at this point rather than commence the next witness. With that great indulgence, we will adjourn now and resume tomorrow at 9.00. That humour not masking the fact that we are already getting concerned about the progress of time in this case. We adjourn now until 9.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 3rd day of February, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.
